content: Maternal administration of glucose during pregnancy has been proposed as a method to enhance the effectiveness of fetal heart rate testing conducted before birth. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits or adverse effects of administering glucose to pregnant women in conjunction with tests designed to assess fetal wellbeing. A comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on July 6, 2012, to identify relevant studies. The review included all randomized controlled trials, whether published or unpublished, that investigated the effects of maternal glucose administration (either orally or intravenously) during pregnancy in conjunction with fetal wellbeing tests. Data extraction and quality assessment of the trials were performed independently by two reviewers. Additionally, the authors of both published and unpublished studies were contacted to obtain further information. The review ultimately included two trials, which collectively involved 708 participants. The findings indicated that administering glucose to pregnant women did not reduce the occurrence of non-reactive results in antenatal cardiotocography tests. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to suggest that antenatal maternal glucose administration decreases the rate of non-reactive cardiotocography results. Further research is necessary to confirm these findings, determine the optimal glucose dosage, and assess the efficacy, predictive accuracy, safety, and perinatal outcomes associated with glucose administration in conjunction with cardiotocography and other fetal wellbeing tests.
